idiom_name: file-scope static state plus accessor functions (module with shared state)
implementation_notes: C has no classes, so the realization moves the state to translation-unit scope: declare the data as file-static variables (or one static struct) in the module's .c file and expose ordinary functions that read and write them, while the handle clients pass around carries no data at all and merely names the module. What replaces the classic structure is exactly the module boundary - static gives the state internal linkage (privacy), the header declares only functions (the instance interface), and static storage duration gives the data program lifetime. Keep the state's definition in one .c file and initialize anything that cannot be a constant initializer through an explicit init function.
pitfalls: Defining the static state in a header (or sharing it through an included .c file) silently produces one copy per translation unit instead of one per program; the definition belongs in exactly one .c file.

There is no encapsulation: every function in the file can reach the state, and nothing prevents a second module from declaring its own copy - route all access through one accessor pair and never export the variable.
File-scope state is shared by all threads; guard it with a mutex (as the EuroPLoP 'software module with global state' pattern prescribes) or make it _Thread_local if per-thread state was the intent.
